result: The manuscript provides background on voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV) and their structural and functional properties, including their role in cellular excitability, their structural similarity to voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV), and the sliding helix model of voltage sensing. The authors note that while structures of NaV channels and CaV1.1 in activated states exist, resting states of eukaryotic CaV and NaV channels remained experimentally inaccessible at the time of the study.
evaluation: Claims C1-C27 and C34 are well-established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims accurately describe the current state of knowledge about voltage-gated calcium channels, their structure, function, and the sliding helix model. The claims are consistent with cited references and represent accepted scientific understanding.

result: A homology model of human CaV1.1 was generated based on the rabbit cryo-EM structure, revealing that the four VSDs differ structurally in helix length and number of gating charges, and can be grouped into two classes (VSDs I/III and VSDs II/IV) based on their countercharge positions in the extracellular negative cluster (ENC). The activated state of VSDs I and III is predicted to be more stabilized than VSDs II and IV based on differences in ion-pair formation.
evaluation: Claims C31-C49 describe the structural modeling approach and structural analysis of CaV1.1 VSDs. The homology modeling methodology is appropriate given the high sequence similarity (92.6% identity) between human and rabbit CaV1.1. The structural observations about VSD differences are supported by the data presented in Figures 1 and supplementary figures. The inference about differential stabilization (C49) is reasonable based on the structural differences in ion-pair formation, though it represents a prediction rather than direct experimental evidence.

result: MD simulation with umbrella sampling and Markov state modeling (MSM) of VSD I revealed four energy minima corresponding to activated and three resting states, with the S4 helix undergoing a stepwise downward movement of 15.3 Å. The gating charges sequentially form ion pairs with countercharges in the intracellular negative cluster (INC) and extensive ionic bonds with the extracellular negative cluster (ENC) in both resting and activated states. Transition times between states occur in the high µs to low ms timescale, with energy barriers of 48-51 kJ/mol in the activating direction.
evaluation: Claims C50-C72 describe the MD simulation and MSM analysis of VSD I. The methodology is appropriate and well-described, using umbrella sampling to overcome energy barriers and MSM to calculate thermodynamics and kinetics. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C68) that absolute transition times may not correspond to physiological values due to the absence of membrane potential in simulations, but note that relative differences are meaningful (C69). The structural predictions are validated by comparison to published structures and by subsequent experimental mutagenesis (see later results). The Chapman-Kolmogorov tests (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) support the reliability of the MSM.

result: MD simulation and MSM of VSD IV (both splice variants IVe and IVa) showed similar basic features to VSD I but with shorter S4 displacement (12.9 Å for IVe, 10.2 Å for IVa), fewer ion-pair interactions, and absence of ion-pair formation by outer gating charges in resting states. VSD IV showed substantially lower energy barriers (35-42 kJ/mol) and transition times 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than VSD I. Alternative splicing of exon 29 affected ion-pair formation in the activated state and modestly affected transition kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C73-C94 describe the MD simulation and MSM analysis of VSD IV splice variants. The structural and kinetic differences between VSDs I and IV are well-documented in the data (Figure 2). The observation that VSD IV lacks stabilizing ion pairs in resting states (C79, C85) is supported by structural analysis. The authors appropriately interpret that calculated transition times primarily reflect kinetic differences rather than voltage dependence differences (C92), which is a reasonable mechanistic interpretation (C93-C94) consistent with the different roles of these parameters in channel gating.

result: Comparison of VSDs I and IV reveals that they utilize structurally distinct ion-pair partners in the ENC: VSD IV uses D1196 in IVS3 (subject to splicing modulation), while VSD I uses E76, E87, and E90 in IS2. VSD I forms ion pairs in both activated and resting states, while VSD IV forms them only in the activated state. The additional ion pairs in VSD I resting states correlate with increased energy barriers and slower transition times, suggesting these interactions determine the slow activation kinetics of VSD I.
evaluation: Claims C95-C100 synthesize the structural and kinetic differences between VSDs I and IV. The structural observations are well-supported by the MD simulation data (Figure 3). The correlation between ion-pair formation in resting states and slower kinetics (C99) is supported by the MSM analysis. The inference that these interactions determine slow activation kinetics (C100) is reasonable based on the data, though it represents a mechanistic hypothesis that requires experimental validation (which is provided in subsequent results).

result: Experimental validation by mutagenesis of E87A/E90A in VSD I resulted in activation kinetics more than 4-fold faster than wildtype, identifying these residues as critical determinants of slow activation kinetics. The mutation also right-shifted voltage dependence by 18.2 mV and somewhat reduced peak current density. MSM analysis of the E87A/E90A mutant showed transition times more than 50-fold faster than wildtype, validating the predictive value of the modeling approach. The authors acknowledge that the magnitude difference between MSM predictions (50-fold) and experimental observations (5-fold) may reflect the limitation that changes in a single VSD affect channel activation according to its contribution to the concerted gating process.
evaluation: Claims C101-C109 describe the experimental validation of the modeling predictions. The electrophysiology data (Figure 4) clearly demonstrate the predicted effects on activation kinetics (C101-C102) and voltage dependence (C103). The MSM analysis of the mutant (C105) shows even larger kinetic effects, validating the modeling approach (C106). The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation (C107-C109) that isolated VSD kinetics may not directly translate to whole-channel kinetics due to the concerted action of all four VSDs. This is a thoughtful interpretation that recognizes the complexity of channel gating while still supporting the main conclusions.

result: Individual mutations E87A and E90A show differential effects on gating properties. E87A right-shifted voltage dependence by 12.3 mV without affecting kinetics, consistent with E87's predicted role in stabilizing the activated state. E90A accelerated activation kinetics 4-5-fold and right-shifted voltage dependence by 7.7 mV, consistent with E90's predicted role in stabilizing both resting and activated states. MSM analysis showed that E90A, but not E87A, greatly accelerated transition times and reduced energy barriers. In both E87A/E90A and E90A mutants, resting states 1 and 2 collapsed into a single energy well, consistent with the loss of sequential E90 interactions with R1, R2, and R3 that stabilize separate resting states in wildtype.
evaluation: Claims C110-C121 describe the differential effects of individual E87A and E90A mutations. The electrophysiology data (Figure 5) clearly demonstrate the predicted differential effects: E87A affects only voltage dependence while E90A affects both kinetics and voltage dependence. The MSM analysis (C116-C121) shows corresponding differences in energy landscapes and transition kinetics. The collapse of resting states 1 and 2 in the E90A mutant (C120) provides strong mechanistic support for the role of E90 in stabilizing multiple resting states. The agreement between structural predictions, MSM analysis, and experimental data across multiple mutants provides robust support for the proposed mechanism.

result: While MSM analysis predicted differences in transition kinetics in both activating and deactivating directions, patch clamp analysis showed that deactivation kinetics were similarly fast (4-10 ms) for wildtype and all mutants, unlike the differential activation kinetics. The authors explain this discrepancy by proposing that activation requires all VSDs to reach the activated state (limited by the slowest VSD), while deactivation occurs when the first essential VSD transits to resting state 2, thus masking the slower return of VSD I to its deepest resting state.
evaluation: Claims C122-C127 address an apparent discrepancy between MSM predictions and experimental observations for deactivation kinetics. The electrophysiology data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) clearly show that deactivation kinetics do not differ between wildtype and mutants (C123-C124). The mechanistic explanation (C125-C127) is a reasonable interpretation that reconciles the MSM predictions with experimental observations by considering the cooperative nature of channel gating. This explanation is consistent with models of voltage-gated channel activation requiring concerted VSD movement, and represents thoughtful consideration of the relationship between individual VSD kinetics and whole-channel behavior.

result: The structure models of CaV1.1 VSDs in activated and resting states fill an important gap in understanding voltage sensing in eukaryotic channels. The two VSDs differ substantially in S4 displacement range and ion-pair formation patterns, corresponding to differences in free energy states and transition kinetics that correlate with experimentally determined gating properties. The combination of MD simulation and MSM proved highly predictive, with all tested interaction partners showing predicted effects experimentally. The structures display basic features of the sliding helix model and closely correspond to recently published cryo-EM structures of homotetrameric NaV channels in resting states, indicating remarkable similarity between eukaryotic CaV1.1 and its bacterial ancestor. The sequential movement of gating charges across the HCS and stabilization by ion pairs with the INC represent highly conserved properties defining the essence of voltage sensing.
evaluation: Claims C128-C140 summarize the main findings and their significance. The claim that the models fill an important gap (C128) is justified given that resting state structures of eukaryotic CaV/NaV channels were not available experimentally (C19). The summary of structural and kinetic differences (C129-C130) is well-supported by the data. The validation of the modeling approach (C131-C133) is demonstrated by the agreement between predictions and experimental results across multiple mutants. The comparison to published NaV structures (C135-C137) provides independent validation, with RMSD values of 1.7-1.9 Å indicating close structural similarity. The identification of conserved (INC interactions) versus variable (ENC interactions) features (C139-C140) represents a well-supported synthesis of the findings.

result: The interactions of outer gating charges with the ENC differ considerably between VSDs I and IV and between VSD IV splice variants. While both VSDs form ion pairs with the ENC, they use partners in different transmembrane segments (IS2 vs. IVS3). In VSD IV, ion pairs are restricted to the activated state, while in VSD I they are also found in resting states 2 and 3, leading to stronger stabilization of resting states. MSM and mutagenesis demonstrated that this stabilization causes dramatic slowing of state transitions and activation kinetics. The negative countercharges in the ENC serve a dual role: enabling hand-over-hand movement of gating charges and stabilizing VSDs in activated states. Mutation of E87 (which stabilizes activated state) perturbed voltage dependence, while mutation of E90 (which stabilizes both resting and activated states) accelerated kinetics and right-shifted voltage dependence.
evaluation: Claims C141-C155 synthesize the mechanistic insights about ENC interactions. The structural differences between VSDs (C141-C145) are well-documented in the data. The correlation between resting state stabilization and slow kinetics (C146-C147) is supported by both MSM analysis and mutagenesis experiments. The proposed dual role of ENC countercharges (C149) is a reasonable mechanistic interpretation supported by the data. The differential effects of E87 and E90 mutations (C150-C154) are clearly demonstrated experimentally and consistent with their predicted structural roles. The consistency with previous mutagenesis studies (C155) provides additional validation.

result: VSD IV establishes stabilizing ion pairs exclusively in the activated state, consistent with its intrinsically fast activation kinetics. Weakening countercharges in IVS3 (by exon 29 insertion or mutagenesis) causes right-shift of voltage dependence with little effect on kinetics. Ion-pair formation of R1 with E87/E90 in VSD I and with D1196 in VSD IV are functionally equivalent in stabilizing the activated state, while ion-pair formation of multiple gating charges with E90 that stabilize resting states is specific to VSD I and represents the structural correlate of CaV1.1 slow activation.
evaluation: Claims C156-C160 synthesize the functional differences between VSDs I and IV. The observation that VSD IV lacks resting state ion pairs (C156) is supported by structural analysis. The inference about fast kinetics (C157) is reasonable based on the correlation between lack of resting state stabilization and fast transitions. The effect of weakening IVS3 countercharges (C158) is supported by previous work (cited). The functional equivalence of different ion-pair partners for activated state stabilization (C159) and the specificity of E90 interactions for slow activation (C160) represent well-supported mechanistic conclusions that integrate structural and functional data.

result: The outward motion of S4 with sequential stabilization of inner gating charges by the INC represents the general theme of voltage sensing, while interactions between outer gating charges and the ENC represent variations on this theme. These interactions differ in number, strength, and position between channels and between VSDs of a single channel. The state in which these interactions are established determines which biophysical properties are modulated. The general principle is that stabilization of VSDs in the activated state shifts voltage dependence to more hyperpolarizing potentials, while ion-bond formation in resting states slows activation kinetics. In CaV1.1, these actions are divided between separate VSDs. The findings provide a molecular mechanism explaining how channels using the same general voltage sensing mechanism can produce distinct gating properties and how distinct VSDs cooperate in establishing characteristic gating properties.
evaluation: Claims C161-C169 present the main conclusions and general principles derived from the study. The distinction between conserved (INC) and variable (ENC) mechanisms (C161-C163) is well-supported by the structural and functional data. The principle that the state-dependence of ENC interactions determines which properties are modulated (C164) is supported by the differential effects of E87 vs. E90 mutations. The general principles about activated state stabilization affecting voltage dependence and resting state stabilization affecting kinetics (C165-C166) are supported by multiple lines of evidence from both VSDs and multiple mutants. The observation that these functions are divided between VSDs in CaV1.1 (C167) is clearly demonstrated. The overall conclusions (C168-C169) represent well-supported synthesis of the findings that advances understanding of voltage-gated channel gating mechanisms.

result: The structure models of activated and resting states of CaV1.1 VSDs I and IV are consistent with the sliding helix model and yielded reliable predictions of the importance of ion-pair formation between outer gating charges and countercharges. The data provide novel insight into how stabilization of VSDs in resting and/or activated states shapes kinetics and voltage dependence of activation, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 summarize the main findings from the abstract. These claims are well-supported by the comprehensive structural modeling, MSM analysis, and experimental validation presented throughout the manuscript. The consistency with the sliding helix model (C28) is demonstrated by the structural features observed. The reliability of predictions (C29) is validated by the agreement between modeling and experimental mutagenesis results. The mechanistic insights (C30) are supported by the correlation between structural features, MSM predictions, and experimental gating properties.

result: Both VSDs displayed typical features of the sliding helix model but greatly differed in ion-pair formation of outer gating charges. Stabilization of the activated state enhanced voltage dependence of activation, while stabilization of resting states slowed kinetics. This mechanism explains how specific ion-pair formation in separate VSDs can realize characteristic gating properties of voltage-gated cation channels.
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are the main conclusions stated in the abstract. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented in the manuscript, including structural modeling (showing sliding helix features and differences in ion-pair formation), MSM analysis (showing correlations between stabilization and kinetics/voltage dependence), and experimental validation (demonstrating predicted effects of mutations). The mechanistic model (C7) represents a well-supported synthesis of the findings.
